title: Manner: behaviour and body language
subtitle: courtesy, etiquette, smirk, flinch
summary: Describe good and bad manners precisely - from courtesy and etiquette to the small non-verbal signals such as smirking, flinching and squirming.

lesson.heading: Polite and impolite
lesson.text: **Courtesy** is politeness and respect, and someone who has it is **courteous**. The opposite is **discourteous** - impolite and lacking respect. If you seem rude because you show no interest in other people, you are being **offhand**; **insolent** is much stronger than discourteous and means openly rude and disrespectful.

examples.text: The teacher said her students were always very **courteous**.
She addressed the customer in a very **discourteous** manner.
I hope I didn't appear **offhand** with her - it's just that I was in such a hurry.
The boy had an **insolent** expression on his face which irritated me.

lesson.heading: Rules of accepted behaviour
lesson.text: **Etiquette** is the set of rules or customs for accepted behaviour in a particular social group or situation, and **netiquette** is the code of behaviour for using the internet. **The done thing** is what you are expected to do socially. To **stand on ceremony** is to behave formally, and someone **straitlaced** has old-fashioned, fixed morals.

examples.text: What's the **etiquette** at a traditional Chinese wedding? I've had an invitation to one.
When taking part in online discussions, always follow **netiquette** and keep your comments brief.
Asking for more food at a formal dinner party is just not **the done thing**.
Here, have a seat. Relax - there's no need to **stand on ceremony**.
My elderly uncle and aunt are both rather **straitlaced**.

lesson.text: **Manners** (the way we behave socially) is always plural - staff with good **manners**, not ~~good manner~~; **manner** in the singular is a formal word for 'way of doing something': He greeted everyone in a friendly **manner**.

lesson.heading: Body language: what the movement shows
rows: surprise or shock (showing it or causing it)
either a person or a piece of behaviour can raise eyebrows
repeated small movements with part of the body
move from side to side in an awkward way
a broad smile, with positive associations
breathe air in through your nose so that it makes a noise
force air quickly up or down your nose, making an explosive sound

lesson.heading: Non-verbal language in use
lesson.text: Research shows that we communicate far more through **body language** and **non-verbal** noises than we realise. Notice that most of these verbs carry a judgement: a person who **beams** looks delightful, while a person who **smirks** looks pleased with themselves in an unattractive way.

examples.text: Jamie was **twitching** all evening - he was clearly nervous, not relaxed.
The dentist stopped drilling as soon as he felt me **flinch**.
Ritva **squirmed** in her chair when Karl said her photo was in the paper.
She **beamed** with happiness all through the wedding ceremony.

lesson.heading: Two noisy noses, two kinds of laugh

left.label: sniff at / snort
left.text: Both use the nose. **Sniff at** something shows disapproval; **snort** is an explosive sound of disgust or great amusement.
examples: Kate **sniffed at** every comment I made at the meeting - she clearly disapproved.
Brendan **snorted** with laughter all through the play.

right.label: titter / beam
right.text: A **titter** is a weak laugh of nervousness or embarrassment - not a compliment to a comedian. A **beam** is a broad, happy smile.
examples: The students **tittered** when the teacher tripped over the wastepaper basket.
There was only an occasional **titter** at the comedian's jokes.

lesson.text: If someone's behaviour **raises eyebrows**, people find it surprising or shocking - so bad table manners at a formal dinner will certainly raise a few.

exercises.prompt: A light kiss on each cheek is the done ___ in some cultures when you meet someone you know.
exercises.explanation: The done thing is what you are expected to do in a social situation.

exercises.prompt: Joanna and David always taught their children to have good ___.
exercises.explanation: Manners, the way we behave socially, is always plural - not good manner.

exercises.prompt: We don't stand on ___ in this house - just help yourself to anything you want from the fridge.
exercises.explanation: To stand on ceremony is to behave in a formal way.

exercises.prompt: Some people don't seem to follow any kind of ___ when posting messages on social network sites, and often post offensive material.
exercises.explanation: Netiquette is the code of behaviour for using the internet.

exercises.prompt: She was very ___ and hardly looked at me when she replied.
exercises.explanation: Offhand means showing a rude lack of interest in others.

exercises.prompt: I'm sick of your ___ comments. It's time you learnt to speak politely to people. You're so rude!
exercises.explanation: Insolent means rude and not showing respect - much stronger than discourteous.

exercises.prompt: For a young person, she's very ___ and old-fashioned in her ideas and behaviour.
exercises.explanation: Someone straitlaced has old-fashioned and fixed morals.

exercises.prompt: Students should always address their teachers in a courteous manner. Anyone who behaves in a ___ way will be reported to the Director.
exercises.explanation: Discourteous means impolite and lacking respect.

exercises.prompt: Brendan ___ with laughter all through the play.
exercises.explanation: Snort can express great amusement as well as disgust; sniffing at something shows disapproval.

exercises.prompt: Whenever I'm tired or nervous, my eyelid starts to ___.
exercises.explanation: Twitch is a repeated small movement of part of the body, showing nervousness.

exercises.prompt: Don't keep ___ in your chair like that - sit still and behave yourself.
exercises.explanation: To squirm is to move from side to side in an awkward way, out of embarrassment or nervousness.

exercises.prompt: The students ___ when the teacher tripped over the wastepaper basket.
exercises.explanation: A titter is a small, nervous or embarrassed laugh.

exercises.statement: If Kate sniffed at every comment you made in a meeting, she approved of what you said.
exercises.explanation: No - to sniff at something shows disapproval. Kate did not like your comments.

exercises.statement: If only an occasional titter greeted a comedian's jokes, the comedian will have been disappointed.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a titter is a weak laugh, more from embarrassment than amusement.

exercises.statement: Meg is smirking and Tanya is beaming, so Tanya has the more pleasant expression.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a beam is a broad, happy smile, while a smirk is a self-satisfied and unattractive one.
